pipeline.backfill_help: Downloads the days missing from the range, one file per step (about 2 MB each), oldest first. EPSS goes back to 14 April 2021. Scores move slowly, so one file a week is usually enough for the distant past; keep one a day for recent months.

news.help: Type of event, firmness and sectors come from keyword rules: they are simple labels and some are wrong. The same story from several feeds is grouped when the titles are close; Italian and English versions are not grouped yet. Published is the publisher's time; First seen is when this system collected the item, the only time used for modelling.

col.title: Title
news.trend_help: Counted by publication day (UTC). This measures press and advisory coverage seen by these feeds, not the number of attacks. A sector is counted when it is mentioned, whether or not it was the target.
vulns.no_data: No vulnerability catalogue yet. Open Pipeline and run NVD.
vulns.as_of: NVD records as last retrieved on {date}
vulns.by_year_help: The current year is still filling up. Counts include every CVE NVD holds, exploited or not.
vulns.vendors_help: A wide product range means more records. This is not a measure of how secure a vendor is.
vulns.lookup_empty: Nothing stored about this CVE yet.
vulns.kev_added: Added to KEV on {date}. Known ransomware use: {ransomware}.

categories.no_data: Nothing to categorise yet: the NVD catalogue has not been downloaded.
categories.coverage_help: Coverage by CVE matters more than by product: a few busy products carry most of the catalogue. The exploited figure is the one to watch, because those are the CVEs the forecasts are about.
categories.summary_help: A CVE affecting products in two categories is counted in both, so the totals add up to more than the number of CVEs. Counts follow how many vulnerabilities were published, not how exposed anyone is.
categories.queue_help: Products no rule recognised, with the ones behind exploited vulnerabilities first. Assigning the first few changes the numbers more than the rest put together.
categories.assign_help: Currently assigned by: {by}. A decision made here always beats the rules and survives a rule change.
forecast.no_data: Not enough catalogue yet: the forecast needs NVD, KEV and the category mapping.
forecast.method: Expected newly exploited vulnerabilities in the next {horizon} days, per category: however many of that category became known-exploited over the last {lookback} months, scaled to the horizon. The bar is the expectation, the line is the range the evidence supports.
forecast.table_help: 'Exploited share' and 'median days' describe the category's history and are not inputs to the number: they say how often and how fast, when it happens.
forecast.rates_help: Share of vulnerabilities exploited within {n} days of publication. Only CVEs published long enough ago to have had those {n} days are counted, so recent ones do not drag the share down.
forecast.speed_help: Counted only over vulnerabilities that were exploited, so this answers how quickly, not how likely. Half of the cases fall between the 25th and 75th day columns.
forecast.limits: What these numbers do not say
forecast.limits_text:
- **Exploitation means the day CISA listed the CVE as exploited.** That is later than the real start and covers what matters to US federal agencies, so every figure here is a floor, not an estimate of all exploitation.
- **The forecast assumes the near future looks like the recent past.** It is a baseline any real model has to beat, not a prediction of a specific attack.
- **Categories overlap**: a CVE affecting a firewall and an operating system counts in both.
- **Nothing here says who attacks or from where**, and no vendor ranking is implied: a wide product range means more vulnerabilities, not worse security.
- **The system sees what its sources see.** A change in the numbers can be a change in coverage rather than a change in the world.

overview.at_risk: Most at risk in the next 90 days
overview.at_risk_help: Vulnerabilities expected to become known-exploited, by technology category.
overview.at_risk_metric: Between {low} and {high}. Historically {share} of this category's vulnerabilities are exploited within 90 days.
overview.at_risk_link: The Forecast section shows every category, how the numbers are built and what they do not say.
forecast.acc_help: Scored month by month from {start} to {end}, each forecast made with only what was known on that day. Average error is in vulnerabilities per category per window; range held is how often the actual number fell inside the interval.
forecast.acc_methods: Other methods scored the same way. The dashboard uses the one at the top; the publication-volume method it shipped with is the one called volume_rate. Every method runs below the truth, because a trailing estimate lags a rising trend.
scans.intro: How much the Internet is being scanned for each kind of service, from the SANS Internet Storm Center. A jump often comes before a vulnerability is confirmed exploited. Aggregated sensor data: no individual address is fetched, stored or shown.
scans.no_data: No scanning data yet. Open Pipeline and run the scanning source, or backfill its history.
scans.surge_line: **{service}** (port {port}, {category}) — {ratio}× its usual level, {z} standard deviations above baseline.
scans.surge_help: Compared with each service's own last 30 days. It means more machines than usual are probing that service now, not that anything has been breached.
scans.no_surge: Nothing is being scanned noticeably more than its own baseline right now.
scans.trend_help: Distinct source IPs seen per day, summed over the ports tied to each category. A port maps to a category only loosely, so read the shape over time, not the absolute height.
scans.about: What this is, and is not
scans.about_text:
- **Source**: the SANS Internet Storm Center (DShield), which aggregates many sensors' logs into daily totals per port. We never fetch or store an individual address.
- **Ports stand in for categories loosely.** Many services share a port and 443 carries almost everything, so this is scanning of services *associated with* a category, not a product and never a target.
- **It is an early signal, not proof.** A surge means attention; it precedes exploitation often enough to be worth watching, but not always, and quiet is not safety.
- **One network of sensors sees a slice of the Internet.** A change can be a change in the sensors as much as in the world.
